texts.preamble: Natar Veettil Lakshmi vs State Of Kerala on 12 January, 2016 Author: B.Sudheendra Kumar Bench: B.Sudheendra Kumar In The High Court Of Kerala At Ernakulam Present: The Honourable Mr. Justice B.Sudheendra Kumar Tuesday, The 12Th Day Of January 2016/22Nd Pousha, 1937 Crl.Rev.Pet.No. 4395 of 2006 ( ) --------------------------------- Crl.A 381/2004 of Addl. Sessions Court (Adhoc-Iii), Kasaragod Cc 191/2000 of J.M.F.C.-Ii,Hosdrug Revision Petitioner/Appellant/Accused 3 & 4:: ----------------------------------------------------------------------- 1. Natar Veettil Lakshmi, Natar Veedu, Periyaram, Kannur. 2. Muthuraj Chips, Periyaram, Rep. By Its Owner Natar Veettil Lakshmi Natar Veedu, Periyaram, Kannur. By Adv. Sri.Blaze K.Jose Respondent/Complainant:: -------------------------------------------- State Of Kerala, Represented By The Public Prosecutor High Court Of Kerala, Ernakulam Representing Food Inspector, Kanjangad Circle. By Public Prosecutor, Shri.R.Githesh This Criminal Revision Petition Having Been Finally Heard On 12-01-2016, The Court On The Same Day Passed The Following: B.Sudheendra Kumar, J. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - -- - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - Natar Veettil Lakshmi vs State Of Kerala on 12 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/197081564/ 1 Crl. texts.facts: The accused Nos.3 and 4 in C.C. No.191 of 2000 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class - II, Hosdurg filed this Revision Petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 16(1) (a) read with Section 2(ia)(j) and 7(i) read with Section 17 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 . 2. Heard. 3. The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:- On 20.12.1999 at 5 p.m., PW3, the Food Inspector, purchased 600 gram of banana chips from the shop of the second accused. First accused was the vendor. Fourth accused was the manufacturer, who supplied the chips to second accused. Third accused was the licensee of fourth accused. After sampling as per rules, one of the samples was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst. The report of the Public analyst would show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for banana chips under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1956 and therefore, the same was adulterated. Thereafter, on the request of the accused, second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. Ext .P21 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would show that the sample contained water soluble synthetic colour in violation of Rule 26 of PFA Rules and therefore, it was adulterated. Thereafter, complaint was filed before the court by the Food Inspector after complying with the legal formalities. 4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW6 were examined and Exts. P1 to P29 series were marked for the prosecution. DW1 was examined and Exts.D1 and D2 were marked for the revision petitioners.
texts.arguments: 5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P21 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument. 6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act. Therefore, Ext. P21 certificate of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex Natar Veettil Lakshmi vs State Of Kerala on 12 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/197081564/ 2 court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra). It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused. The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.
